inputs.need:
I am the clinical nurse educator in a 16-bed medical and surgical intensive care unit. Two years ago we adopted a nurse-driven daily sedation interruption protocol: every morning the bedside nurse screens ventilated patients on continuous sedation for safety criteria and, if they pass, stops the infusion and assesses the patient, then calls the respiratory therapist for a breathing trial. Our last three months of documentation show the safety screen was done on 71 percent of eligible patient-days, the interruption itself on only 38 percent, and the paired breathing trial on 29 percent. The reasons written in the chart are things like agitated overnight, family at the bedside, physician preference and no time before rounds.

We want to use lean methods (value stream mapping, gemba walks at 07:00 and A3 thinking with the bedside nurses and respiratory therapists) to see where the morning process breaks down and to raise completed interruptions to 70 percent of eligible patient-days within six months. I would like help finding what has been published on why these protocols are not followed and on changes that worked, choosing measures that show whether we improve without more self-extubations or distress, and setting up a simple weekly data display the charge nurses can keep up. We have no extra staff, and anything we change has to fit the morning before 09:00 rounds.
inputs.constraints: No additional staff; changes must fit the existing morning workflow before 09:00 rounds; the hospital lean facilitator is available four hours a week from November 2026 to April 2027.

records.title: Adherence to daily spontaneous awakening trials under a nurse-driven protocol: a two-year observational study in three intensive care units
records.authors: Brandvold-Mensah K, Iwasaki-Oyelaran T, Carvalho-Dunn R
records.venue: Journal of Critical Care Nursing Practice
records.abstract: We reviewed 5,940 eligible ventilated patient-days in three intensive care units using a nurse-driven sedation interruption protocol. An awakening trial was performed on 44 percent of eligible days. The most common documented reasons for not performing it were overnight agitation (31 percent of missed days) and planned procedures (18 percent), and 22 percent of missed days had no documented reason. Units that kept a paper checklist at the bedside performed trials on 58 percent of eligible days against 37 percent in the unit without one. Adherence did not change over the two years.

records.title: Pairing awakening and breathing trials: coordination between nurses and respiratory therapists
records.abstract: In one medical intensive care unit, awakening trials by nurses and breathing trials by respiratory therapists were scheduled separately and rarely paired. The unit agreed a shared 08:00 time for both trials and a bedside card that the nurse handed to the therapist when the awakening trial passed. Over nine months the proportion of eligible patient-days with a paired trial rose from 22 percent to 49 percent, and median ventilator days fell from 6.1 to 5.2. The comparison was before and after, and the unit's case mix changed during the period.

records.title: Value stream mapping of the morning sedation interruption process in an intensive care unit
records.abstract: Nurses, respiratory therapists and physicians mapped the morning sedation interruption process in a 20-bed intensive care unit. The map showed 11 steps and four waits, the longest being physician approval before a nurse could stop sedation (median 47 minutes), which often ran into rounds. The team removed the approval step for patients who passed the safety screen and moved the screen to 06:30. Over 16 weeks, completed interruptions on eligible days rose from 35 percent to 63 percent. The evaluation was an uncontrolled before-after comparison without follow-up beyond 16 weeks.

records.title: Why nurses do not interrupt sedation: a qualitative study of decision making at the bedside
records.abstract: We spoke with 21 critical care nurses in two units about mornings when they did not interrupt sedation for an eligible patient. Nurses described fear of self-extubation and of an agitated patient harming themselves, reluctance when family members were present, pressure to have patients ready for rounds, and uncertainty about whether they could stop sedation without a physician's agreement. Several said the protocol's safety screen was clear but that the decision to act on it felt like a personal risk. Nurses with more than five years of experience interrupted sedation more readily.

records.title: Safety of nurse-driven sedation interruption: self-extubation and agitation events across 4,200 interruptions
records.authors: Petrov-Nwosu D, Castellanos-Whitby E, Sato-Mbeki L
records.abstract: We recorded adverse events during 4,200 nurse-driven sedation interruptions in four intensive care units over three years. Self-extubation occurred in 0.6 percent of interruptions and was not more frequent than on days without interruption in the same patients. Agitation requiring a bolus dose occurred in 9 percent of interruptions and usually settled within 30 minutes. No self-extubation led to reintubation after more than one hour. Events were recorded by the bedside nurse, and events on days without interruption may have been under-reported.

records.title: Sedation interruption protocols, adherence and ventilator days: a systematic review
records.authors: Rahman-Ellis T, Lindgren-Obi F, Moreau-Kamara S
records.abstract: We included 17 trials and 12 observational studies of daily sedation interruption or nurse-driven sedation protocols. In trials, daily interruption was associated with fewer ventilator days (mean difference -1.2 days), but adherence in trials was about 80 percent of eligible days, while routine practice studies reported adherence between 30 and 55 percent. Implementation strategies were described in only nine studies and were too varied to compare. The authors conclude that the gap between trial and routine adherence limits the benefit patients receive in practice.

records.title: Electronic reminders for daily sedation interruption: an interrupted time series
records.venue: Journal of Critical Care Nursing Practice
records.abstract: An intensive care unit added an electronic reminder that prompted the bedside nurse at 06:00 to complete the sedation safety screen. In an interrupted time series over 18 months, documented screening rose from 62 percent to 88 percent of eligible days, but completed interruptions changed little, from 36 percent to 39 percent. Chart review showed that nurses documented the screen and then deferred the interruption until after rounds. The authors conclude that reminders improved documentation rather than practice and that the barriers lay later in the morning process.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records from the second search, appraised at abstract level; the first search reported two hits but returned no records, and three model leads remain unchecked. Routine adherence to sedation interruption is far below trial adherence, and the benefit on ventilator days seen in trials depends on it. In the records, the process breaks down after the screen: a reminder improved documentation but not interruptions, and a value stream map found the longest wait at physician approval, whose removal was followed by a large rise in completed interruptions. Nurses describe fear of self-extubation, family presence, pressure before rounds and unclear authority. Self-extubation during interruptions is rare. Coordination of awakening and breathing trials by a shared time raised paired trials in one unit. The evidence supports a local lean redesign aimed at the waits after the screen, with self-extubation and agitation as balancing measures.
response.gradeRationale: Single-unit before-after reports and observational studies with a consistent direction, a review of trials that is indirect for implementation, and one interrupted time series; certainty that a redesign of the morning process raises completed interruptions is low.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded; overall certainty low; three leads remain unverified.

response.reading: The morning process has three hand-offs: the screen, the decision to stop sedation, and the breathing trial. Local data show the loss after the screen (71 to 38 percent) and after the interruption (38 to 29 percent). The retrieved records point to waits for authority and to poor coordination with respiratory therapy rather than to forgotten screens, and a reminder that improved documentation left practice unchanged. Fear of self-extubation drives nurse decisions, although self-extubation is rare.

response.overview: Six-month lean A3 in a 16-bed intensive care unit: an eight-week baseline, value stream mapping with five gemba walks at 07:00, then A3 cycles testing two countermeasures in sequence (removal of the informal approval step for patients who pass the screen, then a shared 08:00 time and hand-off card with respiratory therapy).
response.population: All eligible ventilated patient-days on continuous sedation from September 2026 to April 2027, about 60 a week.
response.exposure: Countermeasure 1 from week 3 of the A3: nurses stop sedation after a passed screen without waiting for physician agreement, with a physician informed at rounds. Countermeasure 2 from week 9: shared 08:00 time and a bedside hand-off card for the breathing trial.
response.procedures: The charge nurse records for each eligible patient-day whether the screen, interruption and breathing trial were completed and the reason if not, on a one-line tally sheet. The facilitator runs the A3 with two bedside nurses, one respiratory therapist and one physician. Self-extubations and agitation needing a bolus during interruptions are recorded from the incident system and the chart. Weekly results are posted on the unit board.

response.designSummary: Weekly run chart of completed interruptions with a p-chart for context, and a days-between-events chart for self-extubation.
response.sampleSize: About nine eligible patients a day give about 60 eligible patient-days a week. At a baseline of 38 percent, a weekly p-chart has three-sigma limits about 19 percentage points either side of the centre line, so single weeks show little; the run chart shift rule (six consecutive weeks above the baseline median) will detect a sustained rise to about 55 percent or more within the six months. Self-extubation during interruptions is expected about once every one to two months (0.6 percent of about 40 interruptions a week), so it is plotted as days between events rather than as a weekly rate.

response.risks: The protocol is already approved practice; the main risk is harm during interruption (self-extubation, agitation), which is monitored and reviewed at every huddle, and blame on individual nurses, which is avoided by reporting unit-level data only.
response.consent: No individual consent: the redesign supports an approved protocol; families are given a short explanation of morning awakening, with an interpreter when needed.
response.data: The tally sheet holds bed number, date and completion only; unit-level weekly data are posted; no patient identifiers leave the unit.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families who do not speak the unit's main language may not understand why their relative is woken, and patients with limited English may be judged agitated when they are frightened. Interpreter access is part of the morning routine and missed interruptions attributed to agitation are reviewed for these patients.
response.effectiveness: Success means a sustained shift in completed interruptions with no rise in self-extubation or rescue boluses.
response.efficiency: About five minutes a day of charge nurse time and the facilitator's four hours a week.
response.partnerships: Bedside nurses, respiratory therapists, the ICU medical director and nurse manager as sponsors, and a family partner from the ICU family advisory group.
response.rebPath: Service improvement of an approved protocol; the hospital's quality office will be asked to confirm that no research ethics review is needed before any publication, following the TCPS 2 guidance on quality improvement.
response.limitations: One unit; before-after design with run charts; documentation may change faster than practice.
response.summary: Low-risk improvement of an approved protocol with safety monitoring and interpreter access.

response.partnershipPlan: A family partner from the ICU family advisory group reviews the explanation given to families; two bedside nurses and one respiratory therapist sit on the A3 team.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comments from the unit's family feedback cards are read for mentions of patients being woken.

response.title: A lean redesign of the morning sedation interruption process in an intensive care unit: an improvement report
response.abstract: Problem: in a 16-bed intensive care unit, sedation was interrupted on 38 percent of eligible patient-days although the safety screen was documented on 71 percent. Intervention: value stream mapping and A3 cycles testing removal of an informal approval step and a shared time with respiratory therapy. Measures: weekly completed interruptions, paired breathing trials, self-extubation and rescue boluses. Results and conclusions will be written after April 2027.
response.introduction: The benefits of daily sedation interruption depend on adherence, which is much lower in routine practice than in trials. In the retrieved records, the process fails after the screen, at waits for authority and hand-offs.
response.methods: Eight-week baseline, value stream mapping with gemba walks, A3 cycles with two countermeasures in sequence, daily tally by the charge nurse, run charts with pre-specified rules and a days-between-events chart for self-extubation; SQUIRE 2.0 reporting.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the value stream map, the run charts with countermeasure dates and the safety charts.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret any shift against the run chart rules, compare the countermeasures with those in the retrieved reports and state what the unit keeps.
response.limitations: One unit; before-after design; possible documentation drift.
response.conclusion: To be written after April 2027; it will be limited to this unit's process measures and will not claim an effect on ventilator days.
response.summary: SQUIRE-structured draft with results left empty until data exist.
